parsed.explanation: The combined operative regime is a self-governing territory whose entry, documents and screening run under the parent state's federal rules, which the dossier does not document as trans-restrictive. Territory-specific law is protective on paper: a human-rights statute covering gender identity, extended by the chief legal officer to transgender students (2017), marriage recognised, and the historic sodomy statute replaced. No traveler-facing restriction, facility ban, custody rule, police targeting or trans violence is documented anywhere in the record. However, the dossier records no enforcement actions, complaints or outcomes under the statute, so protections operate as paper machinery rather than demonstrated recourse, and the education protection rests on an executive interpretation rather than a judicial holding. Thin data in a protective, rule-of-law framework resolves toward the high end but short of jurisdictions with documented functioning enforcement.

federal_state_facilities.interaction: Federal facilities follow the parent regime; not documented either way.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Human-rights statute with gender-identity ground; 2015 superior-court ruling shows courts work against discriminatory official refusals.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Statute is territorial; federal law-enforcement posture undocumented.

minors_guardians.interaction: Applies to education settings within the territory; travel with a minor otherwise undocumented.

street_violence_police_response.interaction: Social climate signals (2017 'setbacks and prospects') are unitemised.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: The record carries no complaints or outcomes under the statute, so whether remedies actually work is unresolved; 2017 reporting on setbacks is unitemised.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Superior court ruled for same-sex couples in 2015, showing courts will vindicate LGBT rights locally; statute text operative.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Open questions (enforcement, social climate) are light per rubric; they cannot out-vote documented protections.

anchor_checks.comparison: The 0.35 anchors show universal, state-imposed traveler-facing exposure (registers, mandatory reporting, screening regimes). This dossier documents no traveler-facing restriction at all; the operative territory-specific rules are protective, so the case is far above that tier.

0.55-B documents recurring secondary screening and discretionary denial at borders. No comparable exposure is documented here, but this dossier also lacks any demonstrated enforcement record, so it cannot reach 0.75+ solely on paper protections plus one court ruling.

0.85-A shows documented functioning enforcement: apologies, discipline, compensation after complaints. This territory has comparable statutory coverage and a favorable court ruling, but zero documented enforcement actions or outcomes, placing it a step below the working-protections tier.

0.75-C couples permissive border practice with a working tribunal remedy. This territory matches on protective law and judicial vindication but documents no border practice at all, sitting slightly below on demonstrated operation.

0.95-A shows routine respectful treatment with active ombuds enforcement. This dossier lacks any record of practice, enforcement or social acceptance beyond statute text and one ruling, so it cannot approach that tier.

parsed.synthesis: The combined regime is one small territory under a parent's federal entry and screening framework, with territorial law adding protective anti-discrimination coverage including gender identity, extended to students by executive interpretation, plus settled marriage recognition and repeal of the old sodomy statute. No traveler-facing exposure of any kind is documented — no facility bans, no document policing, no targeting, no violence record. Weighing per rule 13: no criminal offence, no documented targeting, and documented formal acceptance/protection put this above the latent-statute tier; but protections are shown only as paper plus one 2015 court ruling, with no enforcement actions, complaints, outcomes, or violence data. Open questions (how border screening handles trans visitors, whether the statute operates in practice) are light but real. Thin-data extrapolation from a protective, rule-of-law structure with functioning courts resolves high, not to the midpoint: approximately 0.78.
